body.objective: Students will be able to choose and prepare repertoire.
body.iCan: I can choose and prepare repertoire.
successCriteria: I can choose repertoire that suits my skills and the occasion
I can make a structured practice plan with goals
I can mark interpretive choices in my music
body.hook: Great performers don't just learn the notes. They choose music that shows their strengths, plan their practice like an athlete plans training, and decide what story the piece will tell. Preparation is where performances are won.

study.title: Choose It, Plan It, Own It
study.question: How do musicians choose and prepare repertoire for performance?
study.passage:
Part 1, Choosing (10 minutes): Use these criteria to shortlist two or three pieces:
• Fit: suits my range and current technique, with one or two stretch goals
• Contrast: if performing more than one piece, contrast in tempo, mood or style
• Occasion: length and style suit the audience and event
• Connection: something I want to say with it
Part 2, Map the piece (10 minutes): Mark sections and the hardest passages (circle them). Note the form.
Part 3, Practice plan (15 minutes): Plan four weeks. Each day: warm-up (5 minutes), technical work on circled passages using chunking and slow practice with a metronome, then raise the tempo by 4 bpm when clean three times in a row (15 minutes), then play through for musicality (10 minutes). Record yourself once a week.
Part 4, Interpretation (10 minutes): Mark choices in the music: breaths, dynamics beyond the written ones, tempo flexibility, articulation, and the mood or story of each section.
Part 5, Self-assessment (5 minutes): Rate accuracy, tone, rhythm, expression and stage presence from 1 to 4.
study.source: Original performance preparation task written for this lesson.
discussion: Why choose a piece slightly below your maximum difficulty for a performance?
How does slow practice save time?
What story or mood will your piece tell?

study.product: Submit a repertoire choice with justification, a four-week practice plan and a marked-up score, then perform a work-in-progress for peer feedback.

examples.title: Fit
examples.problem: A piece is far above your level, with three weeks to perform. Choose it?
examples.answer: Probably not; choose something you can perform securely with one stretch goal
examples.explore: When would a hard piece make sense?

examples.title: Chunking
examples.problem: How do you practise a hard four-bar passage?
examples.answer: Slow it down, play it in one-bar chunks, then link them, using a metronome
examples.explore: When do you raise the tempo?

examples.title: Tempo goal
examples.problem: Your target is 120 bpm; you're clean at 96. Using the plan, how many steps to reach it?

examples.title: Interpretation
examples.problem: Mark an interpretive choice for a lyrical melody.
examples.answer: Add a crescendo to the phrase peak and a slight ritardando at the end
examples.explore: How does this change the story?

practice.q: Name three criteria for choosing repertoire.

practice.a: Focused work on weaknesses with feedback.

practice.q: When should you raise the metronome tempo?
practice.a: After playing the passage cleanly three times in a row.
To focus practice where it's most needed.

practice.q: What should a daily practice session include?
practice.a: Warm-up, technical work and musical play-through.

practice.q: Why is playing through a piece repeatedly not efficient practice?
practice.a: It repeats mistakes instead of fixing hard spots.

practice.q: How does contrast help a recital program?
practice.a: It keeps the audience engaged and shows range.

practice.q: How can interpretive choices go beyond the score?
practice.a: Shaping phrases, tempo flexibility and colour within the style.

practice.q: Why choose a piece you can perform securely?
practice.a: Nerves reduce accuracy, so security leaves room for expression.
